blocks.text: In 1964 M. Gell-Mann and George Zweig proposed that none of the hadrons, not even the proton and neutron, are truly fundamental, but are made up of combinations of three more fundamental entities called quarks, or quark flavours. Quarks are considered truly fundamental particles, like leptons. The three quarks originally proposed were named up, down and strange (u, d and s). Presently we know of six quarks, just as there are six leptons, based on a presumed symmetry in nature; the other three are called charm, bottom and top (c, b, t). All quarks have spin and an electric charge that is a fraction of the previously thought smallest charge e on an electron. Quarks are never seen on their own.

All hadrons are considered to be made of combinations of quarks (plus the gluons that hold them together), and their properties are described by their quark content. Mesons consist of a quark-antiquark pair: for example, a pi+ meson is an up quark with an anti-down quark, and a pi0 can be made of u with anti-u. Each baryon consists of three quarks. The proton has the quark composition uud, so its charge quantum number is q(uud) = 2/3 + 2/3 + (-1/3) = +1 (the print writes q(udd) here). The neutron has the composition udd, and q(udd) = 2/3 + (-1/3) + (-1/3) = 0. For the pi+ meson, the up quark has +2/3 and the anti-down quark +1/3, which adds to a charge quantum number of +1.

Not long after the quark theory was proposed, it was suggested that quarks have another property called colour, or colour charge (analogous to electric charge). Each flavour of quark can have one of three colours, usually called red, green and blue; the names colour and flavour have nothing to do with our senses. Antiquarks are coloured antired, antigreen and antiblue. Baryons are made of three quarks, one of each colour (blue + red + green = white, Fig. 12.7a), and antibaryons of antiblue + antired + antigreen (Fig. 12.7b); mesons consist of a quark-antiquark pair of a particular colour and its anticolour. Both baryons and mesons are thus colourless, or white. The strong force between quarks is called the colour force, and the theory of the strong force is called quantum chromodynamics, or QCD, to show that the force acts between colour charges (not between electric charges). The strong force between two hadrons is considered to be a force between the quarks that make them up.

blocks.alt: Three panels. A proton (u u d) and a neutron (u d d) each have three quarks coloured red, green and blue, which together are colourless. An antiproton has three antiquarks (u bar, u bar, d bar) carrying anti-red, anti-green and anti-blue, which are also colourless together.

blocks.text: Beta decay in terms of quarks

When a neutron in the nucleus decays into a proton and an electron (the beta particle), an antineutrino is also produced: n -> p + e- + nu-bar. A neutron with composition udd can convert into a proton with composition uud by changing a down quark into an up quark, so the fundamental decay process is d -> u + e- + nu-bar. A neutron is stable only inside a nucleus; free neutrons decay, with a half-life given in the book as 900 s (Do You Know). As our understanding of the fundamental nature of matter deepens, the quark model not only explains the structure of particles but also gives insight into their interactions.

blocks.prompt: Describe protons and neutrons in terms of their quark composition (comprehensive question 12.6). How do a proton and a neutron convert into each other (short question 12.10)?
blocks.explanation: Proton: two up quarks and one down quark, uud, charge 2/3 + 2/3 - 1/3 = +1. Neutron: one up and two down quarks, udd, charge 2/3 - 1/3 - 1/3 = 0; in each the three quarks carry the three colours, so the particle is colourless. In beta-minus decay a down quark becomes an up quark (d -> u + e- + nu-bar), turning a neutron into a proton; in beta-plus decay an up quark becomes a down quark (u -> d + e+ + nu), turning a proton into a neutron.

items: Gell-Mann and Zweig (1964): hadrons are made of quarks, never seen alone. Six flavours: u (+2/3), d (-1/3), c (+2/3), s (-1/3), t (+2/3), b (-1/3), with antiquarks of opposite charge (Table 12.4).

Baryons: three quarks (proton uud, +1; neutron udd, 0). Mesons: quark + antiquark (pi+ = u + anti-d). Colour: red, green, blue; hadrons colourless; colour force, QCD. Beta decay: d -> u + e- + nu-bar.
